title: SYSK Selects: How Flamethrowers Work
summary: SYSK Selects rerun (host Chuck introduces it as a Saturday pick) on how flamethrowers work. The hosts open with a George Carlin bit about flamethrowers, then trace history from an ancient fifth-century BC tube-and-coal weapon and Byzantine Greek fire (with Chinese double-bellows pumps) through the 1901 German Flammenwerfer design by Richard Fiedler, to the two-tank-plus-butane handheld design, the 1942 napalm thickening, and WWII use on boats and tanks. They cover the two-person crew and high casualty rate, a South African car theft deterrent called the Blaster, and civilian uses like forest prescribed burns. The episode closes with a listener mail about a San Francisco traveler who alters hotel art.

segments.title: Rerun intro and George Carlin flamethrower bit
segments.summary: Chuck introduces this Saturday Selects rerun, mentions Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, and the hosts open the show. Chuck recalls a George Carlin bit about the origins of flamethrowers.

segments.title: Ancient flamethrowers and Greek fire
segments.summary: The hosts describe an early fifth-century BC tube weapon that shot hot coal and sulfur, then Greek fire, a petroleum-based mixture pumped from a reservoir through narrow tubes and used by the Byzantines on ships and city walls around Constantinople.

segments.title: Chinese double bellows pump
segments.summary: The Byzantine device used a single-action bellows that fired only on the downstroke. The Chinese built a double-action bellows that compressed air on both strokes, giving a longer continuous burst.

segments.title: Gunpowder and the thousand-year gap
segments.summary: The hosts say gunpowder ended the flamethrower's use for about a thousand years until German engineers revived the idea before World War I.

segments.title: Modern flamethrower design (Flammenwerfer)
segments.summary: Richard Fiedler, an engineer credited in 1901 with inventing the modern flamethrower, used a three-tank design. Two outer tanks hold fuel and a center tank holds compressed butane, which pushes fuel out and also feeds the igniter. A spark plug lights the butane pilot flame, and a second trigger releases the fuel through a valve plug.

segments.title: Napalm, WWII use, and Zippo flamethrowers
segments.summary: In 1942 the Army Chemical Warfare Service developed napalm, a thickened gasoline that carries farther and sticks and burns longer. Flamethrowers were mounted on PT boats and tanks, with the ignition system nicknamed Zippo flamethrowers.

segments.title: Flamethrower crews, casualties, and civilian uses
segments.summary: Operators worked in two-man teams with a dangerous role, and many did not survive. The hosts discuss a South African car theft deterrent called the Blaster and forestry firefighters using flamethrowers for prescribed burns.

segments.title: Fire breathing and closing notes
segments.summary: Chuck notes that fire breathers use a similar principle by spraying kerosene, and the hosts point listeners to related HowStuffWorks articles.

segments.title: Listener mail: hotel art alterations
segments.summary: A listener named Guy from San Francisco describes altering framed hotel art by adding small details, such as a chicken or a beer bottle. The hosts respond and invite listener mail.
